summary_student.text: Small gas flames of methane and ethylene were burned aboard the International Space Station while an electric field pushed on them. Without gravity pulling hot gas upward, the team could see how electricity alone changes a flame's shape, stability and soot. The record says the work was not done for space fire safety; its uses are cleaner, more efficient burning on Earth and possibly future space combustion devices.

summary_professional.text: Laminar methane and ethylene diffusion flames, diluted with nitrogen, were burned on a gas-jet burner and on the CLD coflow burner in the ACME hardware of the Combustion Integrated Rack. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode above the burner (up to 10 kV differential) imposed an electric field of controlled polarity and strength, while fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, dilution and polarity were varied from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Measured quantities were voltage-current curves (chemi-ion current), flame response time to electric forcing, flame shape, luminosity and soot distribution from high-resolution cameras, chemiluminescence and soot volume fraction from filtered spectral imaging, and radiant emission from thermopile detectors.
